name: Mituku
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Stappers, Leo. 1973. Esquisse de la langue mituku. Tervuren: MRAC (grammar; tonal language, not online)

new_statements.quote: 1. On the surface, a syllable will bear one of four identifiable tones: High, Low, Falling, or Rising; in addition, between two Highs (or a High and a Falling tone), downstep (also known as tone slip) can occur. [...] there is no surface vowel length contrast (and there is no underlying vowel length contrast either, a separate matter), regardless of the source and composition of the surface vowel in question.
new_statements.citation: Goldsmith, John. 2002. Tone in Mituku: How a floating tone nailed down an intermediate level. In J. Durand & B. Laks (eds.), Phonetics, phonology, and cognition, 80-95. Oxford: OUP (quoted from the author's open preprint, https://people.cs.uchicago.edu/~jagoldsm/Papers/)
new_statements.locator: §2 'Some basic facts about Mituku', preprint pp. 4-5 (published chapter pp. 80-95)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mituku is a tone language: every syllable surfaces with H, L, falling or rising tone, with downstep between Highs caused by a floating Low; verb radicals, subject markers, object markers and tense markers each carry lexical H or L (the analysis rejects a H/zero account); contour tones arise only where two underlying vowels merge; there is no vowel-length contrast. No accessible source says anything about word stress or accent in Mituku.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress; the paper's exceptions concern where the floating Low docks (historic past vs optative tense markers, Meeussen's rule, rising-tone absorption).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level verbal tonology (infinitives and finite verb forms) analysed from Stappers 1973's data, not from the author's own fieldwork; the tone facts are Stappers', the analysis is Goldsmith's.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Mituku of the Ponthierville (Ubundu) area between the Lomami and Lualaba (mitu1240; self-name kinyamituku, older keleka). The 1970 texts come from a single informant, Isidore Agbamubi of the village Biimbi. Salumbu 1978 covers the Kesikate dialect under the name Metoko; no separate glottocode exists for it.

sources.quote: 1. On the surface, a syllable will bear one of four identifiable tones: High, Low, Falling, or Rising; in addition, between two Highs (or a High and a Falling tone), downstep (also known as tone slip) can occur. [...] there is no surface vowel length contrast (and there is no underlying vowel length contrast either, a separate matter), regardless of the source and composition of the surface vowel in question.
sources.locator: §2 'Some basic facts about Mituku', preprint pp. 4-5 (published chapter pp. 80-95)
sources.note: Whole paper is a tonal analysis built on Stappers 1973: four surface tones (H, L, falling, rising) plus downstep from a floating L; H/L lexical contrast in every verbal morpheme class; no surface or underlying vowel-length contrast. The words 'stress'/'accent' occur only in general theoretical remarks (metrical grids, accent systems), never applied to Mituku; no word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Grégoire, Claire. 2003. The Bantu languages of the forest. In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu languages, ch. 19. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Mentions Mituku (D13) only in passing for Meinhof's rule (òlà˘–à / mà˘–à 'spear'; kònàmbà vs kòndCtà), metatony in the infinitive and certain tenses, and object prefixes, all drawn from Stappers 1973 (listed in its bibliography as Annales Sciences Humaines 80). No stress statement.

sources.citation: Stappers, Leo & I. Agbamubi. 1970. Textes mituku. Africana Linguistica 4 (Annales MRAC, Sciences humaines 68): 209-222. Tervuren: MRAC.
sources.note: Persée PDF endpoint is behind an altcha challenge; the 14 page images were fetched sources from the renderPage endpoint and scanned (tesseract fra, one at a time). Introduction (p. 211) gives only classification (D13), location (near Ponthierville, between Lomami and Lualaba), informant and clan names, and the names keleka/kinyamituku; texts are tone-marked; nothing on phonology, tone or stress.
